items.title: AI was supposed to unlock unlimited opportunities for indie hackers / solopreneurs.
items.summary:
AI was supposed to unlock unlimited opportunities for indie hackers / solopreneurs. 

It might actually become the thing that kills many of them (i'm part of it)

We’re entering a world where everything is evolving faster and faster.

Most major LLMs are already receiving huge updates almost every month and that pace is only going to accelerate. The smarter these models become, the more they’ll optimize their own costs, improve productivity and allow big AI companies to move into basically every market.

Before, small startups, solopreneurs and indie hackers could survive because there were gaps everywhere.

There were markets, niches and problems that large companies had not addressed. 

And iimo, it wasn’t always because they hadn’t noticed them. Most of the time, they simply didn’t have the time or the resources to focus on them.

They had to prioritize the biggest and most profitable markets.

- 1st, because they had high costs. 
- 2nd, because they often had VCs expecting massive returns. 
They couldn’t afford to spend months building something for micro-niches.

But now, that limitation is slowly disappearing.

With the level of productivity AI gives them, these companies will be able to attack the biggest challenges while also targeting the small niches that used to belong to indie hackers.

And that’s the paradox.

What we thought would unlock thousands of new opportunities for us may become our biggest competitor. Big AI companies will be able to address massive markets, niches and micro-niches at the same time.

They’ll probably acquire smaller companies, launch their own subsidiaries or create new AI-powered products almost overnight, all powered by their own models and infrastructure.

They also need new sources of revenue.

Because of the competition between them, you can see by yourself how past weeks and fast reactions where ridiculous between Fable 5, GPT 5.6 and Kimi K3.
 
They’re already making concessions on pricing & margin lol. 

In reality, many of these companies would probably love to charge us much more, but they can’t because another model or platform is always ready to undercut or outperform them.

So one way to compensate will be to enter more and more markets.

And we’re forgetting another uncomfortable point: we are also giving these models our ideas, our projects, our problems and our strategies.

I’m not saying they’re automatically going to steal every idea you type into a chat. But the more original ideas, use cases and emerging problems people share with these systems, the easier it becomes for the companies behind them to understand where the next opportunities are.

Something that wasn’t originally on their roadmap could eventually become a feature, a product or an entirely new company.

At the same time, the barrier to building products is becoming ridiculously low.

Thousands of new projects can now launch every day. So yes, you already need to move beyond the AI slop. You need better quality, better design, better UX, better support, better execution and a better overall experience.

But quality alone won’t solve the problem.

You’re competing on several levels at the same time.

▶️You’re competing against every other builder launching products.

▶️You’re competing against potential customers who may decide to build the solution themselves because AI makes them believe they can. Some of them will succeed, others won’t. But they may spend months trying before eventually coming back to an existing product.

▶️You’re competing against big AI companies.

▶️And you’re competing for visibility and clicks inside AI chats themselves that will lead to conversion.

People are no longer always going to search on Google, click on your website and convert. They’ll ask ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini or another assistant for the best solution and the products that get recommended will have the highest chance of winning.

So we’re entering an era where margins will become harder to maintain, durable moats will become rarer, and competition will exist everywhere.

Does that mean the era of indie hackers is completely over?

Not necessarily.

I do agree that building one random product and expecting it to generate money forever will become much more difficult. But building a durable company is still possible.

You just need a real moat that you keep improving overtime.

Something that makes you so unique that even if models become capable of building almost anything, they can’t replace your entire business with one feature.

That could be proprietary data, a strong community providing exclusive experiences, unique distribution, deep integrations, network effects, a unique workflow or something that would be too expensive, too slow or simply impossible to replicate.

The problem is that many moats will no longer last for years.

Some will be copied within months or even weeks. Obviously, replacing something like Ahrefs and its entire data infrastructure would still take a huge amount of time and money. But for many smaller SaaS products, the advantage may disappear extremely quickly.

That doesn’t make a moat useless.

A few months of advantage can still be enough to grow, generate revenue and build the next layer of differentiation. But you’ll need to keep upgrading your value instead of assuming the original advantage will protect you forever.

And this changes the traditional indie-hacking approach.

Before, the idea was often to launch many different projects, maintain them more or less and move from one opportunity to another.

I think that model will disappear.

You can still run 5 or 10 projects, ofc. 

But you’ll have to accept that some of them will slowly die. The moment you move your attention elsewhere, the product stops improving, competitors catch up, and the moat that once made it special eventually disappears.

So builders will probably have 2 real options :

- One is to keep launching lots of projects because that’s what they enjoy. Some products will decline, others will die, but new ideas will continuously replace them and keep generating revenue.

- 2nd is to choose one, two or maybe three projects maximum and give them your full attention. Constantly upgrade them, improve UX, create new advantages and keep rebuilding the moat before competitors catch up.

Both approaches can work.

But pretending that you can launch 10 products, barely update them and still keep all the revenue forever probably won’t.

And the famous 80% or 90% net margins we used to see in some SaaS businesses will also become much rarer.

When there were five or ten competitors, customers could understand why one solution deserved to cost $99/mo.

But when there are 100 or 1000 products offering roughly the same promise, the difference becomes much harder to perceive.

Visibility, price, branding and distribution start becoming just as important as product quality.

Even when your product is better, enough competitors will undercut you at $19 or $29 just to capture a small piece of the market. At some point, you’ll probably have to sacrifice part of your margin to remain competitive and continue converting.

So no, indie hacking isn’t dead.

But easy, passive and comfortable indie hacking probably is.

The winners won’t simply be the people who can build products anymore. Almost everyone will be able to build.

The winners will be the ones who can distribute, differentiate, adapt faster than their moat disappears and keep giving people a reason not to replace them.

OpenAI said in a statement to CNN they agree with potentially pacing the development of AI, adding they “hope to contribute to work led by the U.S. government, alongside other labs” on the topic.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman suggested it may be time to slow down AI development in a podcast interview Tuesday. The OpenAI models that broke out of their test environment are fueling “long term questions” about how AI companies should address this new rate of progress. [...] The US government should support an international effort to develop tools that can “deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development,” according to the letter.

More than 1,000 employees from frontier AI companies signed the letter, including the chief scientist of OpenAI, one of the ChatGPT developer’s original cofounders, some of Anthropic’s cofoundersand vice presidents at Meta, Google and others. [...] “[W]e may have to pace the rate of AI development to give ourselves enough time for society to harden around these new capability levels,” Altman said.

Anthropic said in a statement they are “glad to see broad agreement” on the need to potentially slow AI development “so society can prepare.”

Meta declined to comment. Google did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

items.title: Gilbert Strang, a quiet MIT professor, picked up a piece of chalk and explained the one skill standing between you and e
items.summary:
Gilbert Strang, a quiet MIT professor, picked up a piece of chalk and explained the one skill standing between you and every account you have ever blown.

MIT put the entire course online. it has been free for over twenty years. almost nobody finishes it.

His point: the market never pays in certainties. it pays in probabilities, and a human gut can barely hold one straight. the math that holds ten thousand at once, weighs them, and collapses them into a single call is linear algebra. it is the branch Citadel and OpenAI both pay $400K to hire for.

he is not a trading guru. his 18.06 lectures are the most watched math class on the planet.

Skip to where he turns a wall of numbers into one vector. a single object carrying a thousand odds at once, in notation a beginner can follow.

No slides. no jargon. one piece of chalk.

a quant I know rewatches lecture one every year before he sizes a single position.

You do not have a strategy problem. you have a math problem. the fix has been free for two decades, and you are still guessing.

result.actual_text:
Tôi là một trợ lý nghiên cứu có thể giúp bạn:

- **Tìm kiếm trên web**: tra cứu thông tin, tin tức, báo cáo, tài liệu và các nguồn khác qua công cụ `lookup`.
- **Tìm kiếm trên mạng xã hội**: lấy các bài đăng gần đây hoặc phổ biến trên Twitter/X bằng `social_search`, cũng như xem timeline của một tài khoản cụ thể với `timeline`.
- **Lấy nội dung từ URL**: tải và phân tích nội dung tại một địa chỉ web cụ thể qua `fetch`.
- **Tìm kiếm trên GitHub**: tìm các repository, thư viện hoặc dự án mã nguồn mở bằng `github_search`.
- **Tìm bài báo khoa học**: tra cứu các paper qua `papers` với các tiêu chí lọc và sắp xếp.
- **Quản lý thông tin**: trả lời câu hỏi, cung cấp bản tóm tắt, phân tích và so sánh dữ liệu từ các nguồn khác nhau.

Ngoài ra, tôi cũng có thể thực hiện các tác vụ như:

- Lọc và chuẩn hoá các thông tin quan trọng (ví dụ: dùng `topic="news"` cho tin tức, `timeframe="day"` hoặc `"week"` cho thời gian gần nhất).
- Sắp xếp kết quả theo tiêu chí như số sao, lượt fork, ngày cập nhật, hoặc độ liên quan.
- Hỏi đáp nhanh bằng `clarify` khi cần xác nhận hoặc bổ sung thông tin trước khi thực hiện hành động công khai.

Nếu bạn có yêu cầu cụ thể nào (ví dụ: tra cứu một tài khoản Twitter, tìm bài báo về một chủ đề, hoặc lấy nội dung từ một URL), chỉ cần cho tôi biết và tôi sẽ thực hiện ngay.

results.input: Viết giúp mình một hàm Python tính Fibonacci bằng recursion.

result.actual_text:
Dưới đây là một hàm Python простой recursive tính giá trị Fibonacci:

```python
def fibonacci(n: int) -> int:
    """
    Trả về số Fibonacci thứ n (theo chỉ số bắt đầu từ 0).

    Args:
        n: Số nguyên không âm.

    Returns:
        Giá trị Fibonacci thứ n.
    """
    if n < 0:
        raise ValueError("n phải là số nguyên không âm")
    if n == 0:
        return 0
    if n == 1:
        return 1
    # Trường hợp tái gọi đệ quy
    return fibonacci(n - 1) + fibonacci(n - 2)
```

**Ghi chú:**  
- Hàm này dùng cách tính Fibonacci đơn giản bằng cách gọi lại chính nó cho đến khi đạt các trường hợp cơ sở (`n == 0` và `n == 1`).  
- Với giá trị `n` lớn, hàm sẽ thực hiện nhiều phép tính lặp lại và có thể trở nên chậm; nếu cần tối ưu, có thể dùng memoization hoặc phương pháp lặp.  

Bạn có thể dùng hàm này như sau:

```python
print(fibonacci(10))  # Kết quả: 55
```

items.title: One pattern I find useful for working with LLMs is a nice long ramble session. Sometimes the LLM needs more bits to unde
items.summary: One pattern I find useful for working with LLMs is a nice long ramble session. Sometimes the LLM needs more bits to understand what you're trying to achieve, but you're too lazy to type them. In these cases I like to lean back, switch to /voice and just ramble for like 10 minutes, total mess, anything goes, full stream of consciousness. Sometimes I declare it up top, something like "switching to speech recognition sorry for any typos...". Sometimes I turn it into a small interview of a few turns. But I find that the LLMs are somehow very good at reconstructing long incoherent rambles and often their echo of your own tangle of thoughts comes out quite a bit cleaner than what you started with. The result is that you improve the mind meld and have to correct things less from that point on.

items.title: How OpenAI Lost Control of an AI Model—and What ...
items.summary:
OpenAI was evaluating its artificial intelligence models’ ability to exploit vulnerable software when instead the models hacked the infrastructure surrounding the test, broke containment, and attacked a real company, OpenAI revealed on July 21. Observers say this is the first real-world instance of AI doing something researchers have long worried about: a loss-of-control scenario. If the industry fails to learn from it, it is unlikely to be the last. [...] OpenAI did not respond to TIME’s request for comment, but has said it has partnered with Hugging Face to conduct a thorough investigation and will share more details once complete. But perhaps more worryingly, OpenAI is not legally compelled to disclose the incident in the first place. [...] # What happened?

On July 16, Hugging Face said it had been hit by an unusually automated cyberattack. Over the course of a weekend, AI agents carried out thousands of actions across many temporary virtual computers, moving through the company’s internal systems and shifting the infrastructure coordinating the attack between online services to keep it running. Five days later, OpenAI disclosed that its own models were responsible.
